zones.label: Column 1

Consulted as a headword checkpoint after independent scan reading, not as a diplomatic transcription. lines.note: Tada completes empreſtada from f0477's final body row. Taxacu ſuru illustrates borrowing something; the preceding page's catchword must not be duplicated here.
Taxei means a large number of people and is equated with Vôjei. The initial V and circumflex are retained rather than normalized to modern romanization.
Taxi is the verb for adding what is lacking or making complete. The scan has T, not OCR Faxi; per at the edge has no secure printed hyphen.

runs.text: fazer como numero q̃ falta, ou outra couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The verb can complete a deficient number or something else. Q̃ is the printed abbreviation for que; Vt introduces the numerical example below.
Kazu wo tasu, with taita as an alternative listed form, is making up a number. Taita reflects the historical s-verb past, not a misreading requiring tashita.
Feiçoar completes perfeiçoar, completing the two Portuguese expressions for bringing the number to its required total.
Taxi and taxini are glossed as completing or perfecting. The following example illustrates their use with suru.

The example means to add something as a supplement. A separate damaged ink mark after the sentence is not legible as a numeral or word; the draft's unsupported 5 is omitted as a nontextual mark, with this classification left as a nonblocking caveat.
Taxicana describes someone faithful, loyal, or constant. This evaluative sense is the one explicitly supplied by the Portuguese gloss.
Taxicani is identified as the corresponding adverb. The italic Adu. is an editorial grammatical abbreviation, not Japanese text.
Taxicaſa is the abstract noun associated with constancy or reliability. It stands alone on an indented physical line.
Taxin is explained as bechi no kokoro, another heart or intention. The entry's following extension clarifies the disloyal or treacherous sense.

runs.text: Item, Coração de tredo, ou inimigo, ou desle-

lines.note: The additional sense is a traitor's, enemy's, or disloyal person's heart. The line ends in a hyphen after desle-, not the OCR full stop.
Taxin wo sashihasamu is harbouring an ulterior or disloyal intention. Ter o co- is entirely italic, while al completes the preceding Portuguese desleal.
The example is rendered as having a changed or treacherous heart. Ração completes co-ração without moving text between physical rows.
Taxinami initially means preserving or being sparing. The caron in ǒda is visibly retained, even though expectations from other contracted forms could suggest a circumflex.
Mi wo tashinamu is taking proper care of oneself. The Portuguese Ter is wholly italic; conſi- begins consigo across the break.

runs.text: go, com os veſtidos, & com a limpeza del-

lines.note: The care concerns oneself, one's clothing, and its cleanliness. Both divided words continue across the original physical line boundaries.
After completing the clothing example, geinoo wo tashinamu turns to practising one's arts or accomplishments properly. Vſar bẽ begins the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: & com louuor, & a ſeu tempo das artes, &

lines.note: The arts should be exercised commendably and at the appropriate time. The coordinated noun habilidades follows on the next row.

runs.text: habilidades que hum aprendeo, ou tem.

lines.note: The accomplishments are those one has learned or possesses. This completes the description of cultivated practice rather than introducing another example.
A visibly printed paragraph mark introduces the further sense of being careful and vigilant. Restoring that mark recovers the division omitted by the draft.

runs.text: Taxinǒda fito, l, taxinami aru fito.

lines.note: Tashinooda hito and tashinami aru hito are alternative descriptions of a careful or cultivated person. The printed accent and spaced aru phrase are retained.
The person is described as clean, cautious, respectable, and polished. These social qualities explain the Japanese examples without narrowing them to simple tidiness.
The noun Taxinami is explained through care, cultivated manners, and respectability. Policia here concerns ordered or refined conduct, not a police institution.
De completes honeſtidade. The short continuation finishes the abstract-noun gloss and remains separate from the following headword.

runs.text: Lingua que falão entre ſi os feiti-

lines.note: Taxintçu is described as a special language used among practitioners of divination or magic. The gloss, rather than a modern technical meaning inferred from the headword, governs this interpretation.

runs.text: ceiros, ou adiuinhos com os diſcipulos differen-

lines.note: The practitioners use this speech with their disciples. Differen- begins the statement that it differs from ordinary language.

runs.text: te da commũa pera que os outros não entendão.

lines.note: The language differs from common speech so that outsiders will not understand it. Preserve commũa and the printed nasal marks rather than expanding them.

Aicotoba is said to be the more usual and general term for private group speech. The scan contains a paragraph mark omitted by OCR but no period after Aicotoba; the Japanese term functions within the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: por lingua com que algũs ſe entendem em par-

lines.note: The broader term describes language in which some people understand one another privately. Par- continues particular across the original line break.
Ticular completes em particular, privately or among themselves. This closes the explanatory comparison with Aicotoba.
This Taxǒ is a different lineage or descent, explained by Betno ſugime. The visible t corrects OCR Bemno; the checked-coda spelling Bet is not expanded to betçu.

runs.text: O tornar a nacer neste mundo como ima-

lines.note: The next Taxǒ concerns being born again in this world, as attributed by the dictionary to non-Christians. This separate entry is not merged with the preceding lineage sense.
The account introduces taxoo no kiyen, a bond associated with another life. Liã- begins the Portuguese word for a bond or alliance.

runs.text: ça, ou a mizade de outros nacimentos. ¶

lines.note: The explanation is a bond or friendship from other births. Preserve the visibly separated a mizade; Ta- begins another Japanese example.
The divided example continues Taxǒ quǒgô, explained as births or generations over many ages. The gloss itself supplies the long-duration interpretation.

runs.text: tas idades, ou tempo muito comprido.

lines.note: Tas completes muitas, and the gloss adds a very long span of time. This closes the rebirth entry before the distinct quantity word below.

Taxô combines the ideas of much and little, explicitly vouoi and sucunai. The heavily abraded Portuguese word is read as muita rather than OCR neita; the surviving strokes and the repeated contrast below support the choice, but its initial letters are weak.
Ca completes pouca. The gloss also gives the plural contrast many and few, confirming the quantity sense of this Taxô.
Taxo is another place, explained as yono tocoro. The unaccented ending is preserved and distinguishes its printed form from the nearby accented entries.

runs.text: Outra ſeita, ou peſſoa de ou-

lines.note: Taxǔ is another sect or a person belonging to another sect. Both the headword and its Japanese explanation carry carons over u.
The continuation completes another sect or religious profession. The printed double-s ligature is transcribed as ß without the OCR's additional ſ.
Taxu means many owners or masters, explained by amata no nushi. The scan and Japanese phrase support Amatano, not OCR Amaiano.
Nhores completes ſenhores, the second word for owners or masters. This short row belongs to Taxu rather than the following competence entry.
Taxxa denotes an accomplished person, explained by taxxita fito. The Portuguese says skilled in something; the faint g in algũa is restored from the scan.
The maxim says the expert does not reject a manner or means of working. The scan supports qirauazu, not qiranazu; its Portuguese explanation continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: deſtro não requere bõs instrumentos, nem ha mi-

lines.note: Continuing the previous column, the expert does not require good instruments. The phrase ha mi- continues as ha mister, needing something, on the next row.
The expert also needs little equipment. Michino taxxa introduces another example, a person accomplished in a discipline or way.

runs.text: Deſtro, ou perfeito em algũ arte.

lines.note: The example is translated as skilled or perfect in an art. Retain algũ without adding an a merely to match modern expectations about the following noun.

runs.text: Idem. ¶ Item, O que anda bẽ,

lines.note: Taxxana is assigned the same accomplished sense, then a further meaning concerning someone who walks well. The latter description continues below.
Walking lightly or quickly completes the additional physical sense. It is not a separate headword for travel.
Taxxani is the related adverbial form. Its placement is an indented standalone row, consistent with the neighboring derivative forms.
Taxxaſa is the abstract quality associated with being accomplished or physically able. The printed long s remains part of the Japanese form.
Taxxi means becoming perfected or being accomplished. Its Portuguese per is divided from feito without a clearly printed terminal hyphen, which is therefore not supplied.
Feito completes perfeito. The additional transitive sense is fulfilling or perfecting something, illustrated by the following desire example.
Negai wo tassuru is fulfilling a wish. Two long-s types are visible in taſſuru, correcting the draft's single-s taſuru and matching the verb's Japanese morphology.
Taxxite monouo suru means doing something perfectly or expertly. The Portuguese object begins at the end of this row and continues below.
Couſa perfeitamente completes the explanation of performing an action perfectly. This short continuation closes Taxxi before the ease entry.
Tayaſui means easy. The brief Portuguese gloss does not imply a separate moral or evaluative sense.
Tayasǔ is explicitly the adverb easily. Preserve its round s and the caron over u rather than making the s match the adjacent forms.
Tayaſuſa is the abstract noun ease. Both long-s letters remain as printed in this standalone derivative.
Tayaxi is causing something to cease or interrupting its continuation. The following examples concern ending a lineage and destroying a root.

Per completes interromper. Shison wo tayasu introduces ending one's descendants or lineage; the line is physically indented like the surrounding continuations, despite the draft's flush-left metadata.

runs.text: Fazer ceßar, ou acabar a gèração, ou

lines.note: Su completes tayasu. The Portuguese explains causing a generation or line of descent to cease or end, with another application following below.
The first explanation also mentions a branch of a sect. Ne wo tayasu begins destroying a root; the visible t in ſeita corrects OCR ſeira.

runs.text: ſtruir, ou arrancar a raiz da aruore, &c.

lines.note: The literal example is destroying or pulling out a tree's root. Struir completes De-ſtruir at the preceding line end.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Deſtruir a couſa de raiz.

lines.note: The figurative sense is destroying something at its root. The scan supports Deſtruir rather than OCR Deſtrair, consistent with the explicit root image.
Taye is coming completely to an end or ceasing. The faint initial c of ceſſar is restored; its absence in OCR did not represent a separate historical word.
Naka ga tayuru illustrates a friendship or relationship breaking off. The Portuguese amiza- continues into amizade on the following row.
After completing amizade, michi ga tayuru introduces roads becoming cut off. The Portuguese begins with Tomarſe and continues its alternative explanation below.
The blocked-roads example continues here; the following example begins inochi ga tayuru, the ending of a life. The line-final ta- belongs to that Japanese verb.
Life comes to an end, explicitly explained as dying. The Japanese verb completes across the preceding line break; the explanatory i is followed by a visible comma, not the draft's period.
Iki ga tayuru means that breath fails; the initial of follego is an f, not a long s. The next example begins ato ga tayuru, concerning failure of succession.
The lack of an heir or successor explains the preceding ato ga tayuru. This line starts with ga tayuru in the scan; the doubled c in the historical spelling of successor is visible.
Tayedaye describes intermittent or dwindling continuity. The example is Tayedayeni naru; the draft's o in that repetition is corrected to the visible e.
The Portuguese explains a gradual decrease or reduction. The printed separation a poucando is retained rather than silently replacing it with a modern word division.
Tayegatai is difficult to endure. A separate example starts at the end of the line and continues with suffering on the next row.

The example means unbearable suffering, and curuximi has m rather than the draft's n. The crowded Portuguese adjective is read inſofriueis, with a weakly formed medial u; this chosen reading is less certain than the surrounding words.
Tayegatasa is the corresponding abstract noun, the quality or degree of being difficult to endure. It is a separate indented physical row, not another headword at the column margin.
Tayegatǒ supplies the adverbial form corresponding to tayegatai. The marked final long vowel and its separate indented row are retained.

Tayeiri is explained as fainting or losing consciousness. The conjugational element is ru, not ſu, and the Portuguese fo- visibly breaks across the line. The scan and aligned draft support single-t ita, although the type is not fully crisp; NINJAL's itta is not imported.
The continuation completes fora de si, being beside oneself or unconscious. The printed joining deſi is retained.
Tayema is an interval or interruption. The example starts with fuxin, works or construction, divided Fu-/xin across the physical rows.
Fuxin no tayema ga nai says that the works have no interval of cessation. The Portuguese negation and the repeated idea of interruption agree with the Japanese.
The gloss completes the assertion that the works do not stop or break off. This is a continuation, not an independent entry.
Tayena and tayenaru describe something wondrous or ineffable. The last letters are ine, continuing inefauel on the next line; no secure line-final hyphen is supplied.
Fauel completes the adjective ineffable. The upright S. marks written usage according to the supplied dictionary key; Vt then introduces the example beginning with a wonderful fragrance.
Iro and coye extend the example to color and voice. The Portuguese repeats that these are excellent and wonderful; marauilho- is one word, not the OCR's separated mar auilho-.
The continuation lists fragrance, color, and voice in the same order as the Japanese examples. The s at the beginning completes marauilhoſo across the row break.
Tayeni is explicitly the adverbial derivative. Its indentation and separate line are preserved.

runs.text: Tayexi, ſu, eita. l, tayaxi, ſu.

lines.note: Tayexi and the alternative tayaxi mean to destroy or bring to an end. The alternative starts with t, not the OCR r; eita remains unchanged. The baseline st transcription in Destruir is retained because the joined italic types do not securely establish a long s.
The second Portuguese equivalent is to cause cessation. The entry ends here, before the following verb of silent endurance.

Tayexinobi means to endure silently. The damaged consonant is read b, consistent with the visible stem and the u/ôda conjugation, rather than the draft's f; the final mark is an ampersand, continuing with não on f0479.
